screens.title: Deploying Fabric on Kubernetes — Concepts & Setup
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build a conceptual foundation for running Hyperledger Fabric on Kubernetes. We begin by looking at why Kubernetes is the platform of choice for production blockchain networks, not just another way to run containers. You will learn the concrete benefits Kubernetes brings — automatic recovery, horizontal scaling, rolling upgrades, and a declarative model for desired state — and how those map to Fabric concerns like peers, orderers, and persistent ledger storage. Then we preview the core Kubernetes primitives you must master: Pods, Deployments, Services, Persistent Volumes and Claims, ConfigMaps, and Secrets. You will also see practical setup options for developers: Minikube and Kind for local testing, and the basic steps to connect kubectl to a remote, managed cluster in the cloud. By the end of this chapter you should understand when to move from Docker Compose to Kubernetes and have a hands-on plan to start a local cluster and deploy a simple test application. Think about one production requirement in your environment — high availability, data persistence, or external access — and keep that in mind as we cover each primitive, because Kubernetes gives explicit tools to address each need.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Deploying Fabric on K8s
Deploying Fabric on Kubernetes
Part 1 — Concepts & setup for development and production

Kubernetes automates deployment, scaling, and self-healing of containerized applications. For Fabric this translates into reliable peer and orderer operations, automatic restarts, and controlled rolling upgrades for minimal downtime. In the coming screens we translate these platform capabilities into concrete Fabric practices and show how to start a local cluster for hands-on testing.

Explore Key Topics
K8s vs Compose
Why Kubernetes gives HA, scaling, and declarative control needed for production Fabric.
Core Primitives
Pods, Deployments, Services, PV/PVC, ConfigMaps and Secrets and their Fabric roles.
Local Dev Flow
Using Minikube or Kind to iterate locally before moving to a managed cluster.
Coming up: a practical Nginx deployment lab that demonstrates Deployments, Services, and persistent storage mechanics you will use for Fabric.
Resilience & Scaling
Automatic restarts, replicas, and rolling updates keep Fabric services available.
Configuration & Secrets
ConfigMaps for settings and Secrets for TLS keys and sensitive credentials.
Persistent Storage
PVs and PVCs ensure ledger data survives Pod restarts or rescheduling.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives translate into hands-on skills you can demonstrate immediately. You will practice creating a local Kubernetes cluster and running a sample Nginx deployment to observe Deployments, Pods, and Services in action. You will declare and apply YAML manifests, verify Pod replicas and Service endpoints with kubectl, and clean up resources afterward. Additionally, you will practice creating ConfigMaps and injecting configuration into containers, and you will learn the correct use of Secrets to handle TLS credentials and private keys for Fabric. Finally, you will exercise persistent storage by attaching a Persistent Volume Claim to a Pod so that ledger-like data persists across restarts. Each of these skills maps to a verified competency milestone: a working Minikube cluster, a two-replica Nginx Deployment, a reachable NodePort Service, and a persistent claim that survives Pod deletion. These milestones are actionable checks that show you can operate Fabric infrastructure on Kubernetes with confidence.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Skills & Milestones
Verification Steps
  1. Start Minikube or Kind and run kubectl get nodes to confirm readiness.
  2. Apply a Deployment manifest to create two Nginx replicas and observe Pod scheduling.
  3. Create a Service to expose the app and confirm external access using Minikube service URL.
  4. Attach a PVC to a Pod and verify data persists after Pod restart.
Common Pitfalls
  • Assuming Docker Compose persistence is equivalent to PVs—PVs survive Pod re-scheduling across nodes.
  • Storing TLS keys in plain ConfigMaps instead of using Secrets—ConfigMaps are not secure for private keys.
  • Exposing internal Fabric services with a public LoadBalancer by default—use ClusterIP for internal cluster traffic.

screens.title: Docker Compose vs Kubernetes for Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: Docker Compose is comfortable for local Fabric development: it orchestrates containers on a single host, is easy to read, and is fast to iterate. However, it lacks several capabilities required for production-grade blockchain networks. Kubernetes adds automation for node-level failures, scaling across multiple hosts, rolling upgrades with no single-point downtime, and a declarative desired-state model that operators can rely on. For example, a Fabric Peer contains ledger state and endorsement logic. With Compose, if the host fails you must manually restore containers and storage. With Kubernetes, Deployments and PVCs ensure replicas are recreated and storage remains available. Another difference is networking: Compose exposes fixed container ports on one host, but Fabric in production often needs internal cluster traffic separated from external client access; Kubernetes Services provide stable DNS and IPs even when Pods are rescheduled. A common misconception is that Kubernetes is only useful at huge scale; in fact, the self-healing and declarative operators it provides are valuable for mid-size Fabric networks too. In practice you will often start with Compose for rapid prototyping and graduate to Kubernetes when you need high availability, persistent storage guarantees, and robust operational tooling.

keyIdea.title: Why move to K8s
keyIdea.text: Kubernetes supplies the operational guarantees—self-healing, scaling, stable networking, and persistent storage—necessary for production Fabric networks, beyond what Docker Compose can provide.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Compose vs K8s
Side-by-side comparison
Docker Compose
  • Single-host orchestration
  • Simple development workflows
  • No built-in self-healing across hosts
Kubernetes
  • Multi-node orchestration and scaling
  • Self-healing and rolling updates
  • Persistent storage and stable Services
Concrete example
If a peer Pod crashes, Kubernetes will recreate it and re-attach the same Persistent Volume using a PVC. With Compose you must detect the failure and restore the container and volume manually. That automation reduces downtime and risk for Fabric ledgers.
Operator takeaway
Adopt Kubernetes when you need consistent availability, automated recovery, and a declarative way to manage the lifecycle of peers, orderers, and supporting services. Use Compose only for fast local prototypes.
Common misconception
Kubernetes is not only for very large clusters. Even moderate Fabric deployments benefit from self-healing and persistent volume management.

screens.title: Kubernetes Primitives for Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: Kubernetes expresses infrastructure through a few core primitives you will use repeatedly with Fabric. A Pod is the smallest deployable unit; it usually contains a single container for a peer, orderer, or CA, and shares storage and network resources. A Deployment manages a set of identical Pods, ensuring a desired number of replicas and enabling rolling updates to replace Pods with new versions without downtime. A Service provides a stable IP and DNS name for a group of Pods, so clients can connect reliably even when Pods move. Persistent Volumes and Persistent Volume Claims provide durable storage. For Fabric, attach a PVC to a peer Pod so the ledger and state database survive restarts. ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration like core. yaml settings, while Secrets handle sensitive data such as TLS certificates and private keys and are designed for safer consumption by Pods. Each primitive addresses a specific operational need: Pods run processes, Deployments maintain replicas and updates, Services offer stable networking, PV/PVC preserve data durability, and ConfigMaps/Secrets manage configuration and credentials. Misusing a ConfigMap for private keys is a common pitfall; always use Secrets for sensitive material. Keep these mappings in mind as you design Fabric manifests.

keyIdea.title: Primitive mapping
keyIdea.text: Each Kubernetes primitive has a clear role in Fabric: Pod runs the component, Deployment maintains availability, Service stabilizes networking, PV/PVC preserve ledger data, ConfigMaps and Secrets manage configuration and credentials.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › K8s Primitives
Definitions and Fabric relevance
Pod
Smallest unit, runs a peer or orderer container and its local mounts. Use Pods to encapsulate single Fabric components.
Deployment
Ensures a desired number of peer replicas, performs rolling updates to replace Pods gracefully.
Service
Provides a stable DNS and IP for peers or orderers so clients can reach them regardless of Pod IP changes.
Storage & configuration
PV / PVC
Persistent volumes and claims provide durable storage for ledger files and state databases so data survives Pod restarts.
ConfigMap
Non-sensitive configuration like core.yaml can be injected into Pods as files or environment variables.
Secret
Store TLS certificates and private keys securely and mount them into Pods. Do not store private keys in ConfigMaps.

screens.title: Deployments and Pods — a practical YAML example
screens.narratorSegment: A Deployment is the Kubernetes object that manages a ReplicaSet of Pods. It declares the desired replica count and the Pod template, and Kubernetes takes care of creating and replacing Pods to reach that state. This behavior is essential for Fabric peers: a Deployment can ensure multiple peer replicas exist and can perform a rolling update when you change the container image or configuration. To ground this idea, we'll walk through a simple Nginx Deployment manifest you will use in the lab. The manifest sets replicas to two, declares a selector matching labels, and provides a Pod template with container image and port. After applying the manifest with kubectl, you can confirm two Pods are running and then inspect the Deployment status to observe how Kubernetes reconciles the desired state with reality. A common misconception is that a Deployment immediately scales storage or network configuration—Deployments manage Pods; storage is attached through PVCs and network stability is provided by Services. In short, use Deployments to maintain availability, and combine them with PVCs and Services to provide durable storage and stable endpoints for Fabric components.

keyIdea.title: Deployment role
keyIdea.text: Deployments declare desired replica counts and Pod templates; Kubernetes reconciles the live cluster to match that declaration and enables rolling updates for minimal disruption.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Deployments & Pods
Key behavior
  • Deployments define the desired state: replicas and Pod template.
  • Kubernetes will create or replace Pods to match that state and manages rolling updates.
  • Use Deployments for peers that can run in replicated mode; combine with PVCs for storage.
Concrete example
Apply the YAML below, then run kubectl get deployments and kubectl get pods -l app=nginx to observe two replicas running.
nginx-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
Use kubectl apply -f nginx-deployment.yaml and then check status with kubectl get pods -l app=nginx.

screens.title: Services and Networking in Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: Networking in Kubernetes is intentional: Pods have ephemeral IPs, so Services provide stable endpoints to reach applications reliably. For Fabric, internal component communication should usually use ClusterIP services, which are only reachable within the cluster and are ideal for peer-to-peer and orderer traffic. When you need external access, such as for client applications or a CA endpoint, NodePort or LoadBalancer service types expose the application outside the cluster. NodePort opens a high-numbered port on every node, while LoadBalancer instructs the cloud provider to provision an external load balancer. A practical example from the hands-on activity uses a Service of type NodePort to access the Nginx Deployment. A common misconception is to expose all Fabric components externally; instead, keep internal Fabric traffic internal and only expose required endpoints. Services also enable DNS names and stable selectors, so even if Pods are rescheduled to different nodes with new IPs, the Service preserves connectivity and simplifies configuration of client applications and other Fabric components. Services and Networking in Fabric means use clusterip for internal fabric communications and nodeport/loadbalancer only when external client access is necessary; services keep connectivity stable despite pod churn.. In practical terms, clusterip, nodeport, and loadbalancer for internal and external access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Services & Networking
Service types and use cases
ClusterIP
Default. Use for internal Fabric traffic between peers, orderers, and CAs.
NodePort
Expose a port on every node. Useful for local testing or simple external access to a CA or admin interface.
LoadBalancer
Ask the cloud provider to allocate an external load balancer for production-grade external access.
Example Service manifest
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
  type: NodePort
After creating a NodePort Service you can retrieve the external URL in Minikube using minikube service nginx-service --url. For Fabric, prefer ClusterIP for intra-network connections and carefully expose only required endpoints.

screens.title: Persistent Volumes and Claims
screens.narratorSegment: Persistent Volumes and Persistent Volume Claims are the mechanism Kubernetes provides to decouple storage from ephemeral Pods. A Persistent Volume is a piece of storage in the cluster provisioned by an administrator or dynamically provisioned by storage classes. A Persistent Volume Claim is a request for storage made by a Pod. For Fabric this is critical because ledger files and state databases must survive Pod restarts or Pod rescheduling to other nodes. When a peer Pod mounts a PVC, the cluster ensures the same storage is reattached when the Pod is recreated, preserving ledger continuity. A common misconception is assuming ephemeral container storage is enough; ephemeral storage is lost when a Pod terminates. Design-wise, choose a storage class that matches your durability needs and ensure PVs are sized and backed up appropriately. During testing with Minikube or Kind, you will use local provisioners, but in production managed clusters you will rely on cloud-backed storage classes pointing to durable block or file services. Always verify that the PVC binds successfully before trusting it for ledger persistence. Persistent Volumes and Claims means attach a pvc to peer pods so ledger and state data are stored on a persistent volume that survives pod lifecycle events and node changes.. In practical terms, ensuring ledger data survives pod restarts and rescheduling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Attach a PVC to peer Pods so ledger and state data are stored on a Persistent Volume that survives Pod lifecycle events and node changes.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › PV & PVC
Why PV/PVC matter for Fabric
  • Ledger and state database must persist beyond the life of any single Pod.
  • PVC requests storage and the cluster binds it to a PV, which remains independent of Pods.
  • When a Peer Pod is recreated, Kubernetes reattaches the PV so ledger data remains intact.
Design tips
Choose a storage class that provides the required durability. For local testing Minikube offers hostPath or dynamic provisioners; in production use cloud block or file storage mapped to PVs. Validate that PVC reaches Bound state before relying on it for ledger writes.
Common mistake
Relying on container filesystem for ledger data. Ephemeral storage is lost when the Pod is removed; always use PV/PVC for critical state.

screens.title: ConfigMaps and Secrets
screens.narratorSegment: ConfigMaps and Secrets let you inject configuration into Pods without baking it into container images. ConfigMaps are intended for non-sensitive key-value pairs like core. yaml or orderer settings; mount them as files or expose them as environment variables. Secrets are similar in structure but are designed for sensitive data: TLS certificates, private keys, and database credentials. Secrets are not encrypted by Kubernetes by default unless you enable additional features, but they are handled differently from ConfigMaps and reduce the chance of accidentally committing secrets into code. For Fabric, place node TLS materials and private keys in Secrets and mount them into the peer or orderer containers. A common pitfall is placing private keys in a ConfigMap or code repository; that creates a security exposure. When designing manifests, reference Secrets in Pod specs and enforce RBAC so only necessary operators can view or mount them. Managing rotation, encryption at rest, and secure delivery of Secrets is part of operational hardening for production Fabric deployments. ConfigMaps and Secrets means use configmaps for non-sensitive configuration and secrets for tls certificates and private keys; treat secrets with stricter operational controls and rotation policies.. In practical terms, managing configuration and sensitive material securely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › ConfigMaps & Secrets
ConfigMap
Store non-sensitive configuration data and inject it into Pods as files or environment variables. Useful for core.yaml, logging levels, or feature flags.
Usage tip
Keep configuration declarative and separate from images so you can update behavior without rebuilding containers.
Secret
Store TLS certs, private keys, and credentials. Mount into Pods as files or read as environment variables with restricted access.
Security note
Do not store private keys in ConfigMaps or code repositories. Plan for secret rotation and limit RBAC access to secrets in production.
Concrete Fabric example
Place node TLS certificates and MSP private keys in Secrets, and mount them into peer Pods so Fabric components can perform TLS handshakes and sign transactions securely.

screens.title: Local cluster setup with Minikube or Kind
screens.narratorSegment: To practice Fabric on Kubernetes you should start with a local cluster. Two common tools are Minikube and Kind. Minikube runs a single-node cluster inside a VM or container on your workstation, while Kind runs Kubernetes clusters using Docker containers as nodes. The basic steps are straightforward: install the chosen binary and prerequisites, start the cluster, and verify node readiness. For Minikube you run minikube start; for Kind you run kind create cluster. After the cluster is running, use kubectl cluster-info and kubectl get nodes to confirm connectivity. Then apply the nginx Deployment and Service manifests provided in the hands-on activity. You will use kubectl apply -f nginx-deployment. yaml and kubectl apply -f nginx-service. yaml, then check pods and the service URL with minikube service --url or by inspecting NodePort. Remember to delete resources when finished to keep the environment clean. A misconception to avoid is assuming local clusters behave exactly like cloud-managed clusters; they are excellent for learning and testing, but storage classes and load balancer behaviors differ in production. Still, the local workflow gives you the exact kubectl and manifest experience you need to translate to a managed cluster later.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Local Cluster Setup
Quick start steps
  1. Install Minikube or Kind and required hypervisor or Docker.
  2. Start the cluster: minikube start or kind create cluster.
  3. Verify with kubectl cluster-info and kubectl get nodes.

Command examples
minikube start
kubectl cluster-info

kubectl apply -f nginx-deployment.yaml

screens.title: Connecting to Remote Clusters & YAML Manifests
screens.narratorSegment: Moving from local to remote clusters typically involves configuring kubectl with the correct kubeconfig credentials. Managed services in the cloud such as AWS EKS, Azure AKS, or Google GKE simplify cluster creation and provide provider-specific CLI tools to update kubeconfig. For example, a cloud CLI can download or merge a kubeconfig file so kubectl points to the managed cluster; once configured, kubectl get nodes should list the cluster nodes. From there, you deploy Fabric components by applying declarative YAML manifests that describe desired state for Deployments, Services, PVCs, ConfigMaps, and Secrets. The YAML files should declare metadata, selectors, replicas, container images, and volume mounts for persistent storage. A crucial distinction is that manifests are declarative: you state desired state and Kubernetes reconciles to that state. Test manifests locally in Minikube or Kind, then adapt storage classes and Service types for the cloud environment before applying them to production. A common misconception is that kubectl directly provisions cloud resources; kubectl controls the cluster you point it to, while cloud providers supply the infrastructure and storage classes behind those manifests. Always verify the cluster context before applying production changes.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Remote Clusters & YAML
Configuring kubectl
After creating a managed cluster you typically download or merge a kubeconfig file so kubectl points to that cluster. For some providers a CLI command updates kubeconfig automatically. Validate the connection with kubectl get nodes.

Confirm you are in the correct context before applying manifests to avoid accidental changes in the wrong cluster.

Manifests declare apiVersion, kind, metadata, and spec. For Fabric include Deployments for peers, Services for access, PVCs for storage, and Secrets/ConfigMaps for configuration and credentials. Test locally and then adapt storage classes and Service types for the cloud provider.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the essential concepts to retain. Third, Persistent Volumes and Persistent Volume Claims ensure ledger and state data persist across Pod restarts, preventing data loss. Keep these ideas in mind as the foundation for designing Fabric deployments on Kubernetes and as checkpoints when you translate local manifests to cloud environments. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build a conceptual foundation for running Hyperledger Fabric on Kubernetes. We begin by looking at why Kubernetes is the platform of choice for production blockchain networks, not just another way to run containers. You will learn the concrete benefits Kubernetes brings — automatic recovery, horizontal scaling, rolling upgrades, and a declarative model for desired state — and how those map to Fabric concerns like peers, orderers, and persistent ledger storage. Then we preview the core Kubernetes primitives you must master: Pods, Deployments, Services, Persistent Volumes and Claims, ConfigMaps, and Secrets. You will also see practical setup options for developers: Minikube and Kind for local testing, and the basic steps to connect kubectl to a remote, managed cluster in the cloud. By the end of this chapter you should understand when to move from Docker Compose to Kubernetes and have a hands-on plan to start a local cluster and deploy a simple test application. Think about one production requirement in your environment — high availability, data persistence, or external access — and keep that in mind as we cover each primitive, because Kubernetes gives explicit tools to address each need.

This chapter has focused, practical objectives to move you from local experimentation to production-ready thinking. First, you will be able to explain the advantages of deploying Fabric on Kubernetes, identifying how features like self-healing, scaling, and declarative state solve common operational problems for blockchain networks. Second, you will identify and describe the core Kubernetes primitives—Pods, Deployments, Services, Persistent Volumes and Claims, ConfigMaps, and Secrets—and map each primitive to a Fabric use case such as peer persistence or certificate distribution. These goals help you reason about design trade-offs and operational controls. In examples we will show how a Deployment keeps a peer replica running and how a Service provides a stable endpoint, so you can recognize when to use each primitive. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone so you can check readiness: being able to explain why a PVC protects ledger data, or demonstrating a successful Minikube cluster and a basic Nginx deployment. Aim to complete the hands-on activity in this chapter to validate the skills described here.

These objectives translate into hands-on skills you can demonstrate immediately. You will practice creating a local Kubernetes cluster and running a sample Nginx deployment to observe Deployments, Pods, and Services in action. You will declare and apply YAML manifests, verify Pod replicas and Service endpoints with kubectl, and clean up resources afterward. Additionally, you will practice creating ConfigMaps and injecting configuration into containers, and you will learn the correct use of Secrets to handle TLS credentials and private keys for Fabric. Finally, you will exercise persistent storage by attaching a Persistent Volume Claim to a Pod so that ledger-like data persists across restarts. Each of these skills maps to a verified competency milestone: a working Minikube cluster, a two-replica Nginx Deployment, a reachable NodePort Service, and a persistent claim that survives Pod deletion. These milestones are actionable checks that show you can operate Fabric infrastructure on Kubernetes with confidence.

Docker Compose is comfortable for local Fabric development: it orchestrates containers on a single host, is easy to read, and is fast to iterate. However, it lacks several capabilities required for production-grade blockchain networks. Kubernetes adds automation for node-level failures, scaling across multiple hosts, rolling upgrades with no single-point downtime, and a declarative desired-state model that operators can rely on. For example, a Fabric Peer contains ledger state and endorsement logic. With Compose, if the host fails you must manually restore containers and storage. With Kubernetes, Deployments and PVCs ensure replicas are recreated and storage remains available. Another difference is networking: Compose exposes fixed container ports on one host, but Fabric in production often needs internal cluster traffic separated from external client access; Kubernetes Services provide stable DNS and IPs even when Pods are rescheduled. A common misconception is that Kubernetes is only useful at huge scale; in fact, the self-healing and declarative operators it provides are valuable for mid-size Fabric networks too. In practice you will often start with Compose for rapid prototyping and graduate to Kubernetes when you need high availability, persistent storage guarantees, and robust operational tooling.

Kubernetes expresses infrastructure through a few core primitives you will use repeatedly with Fabric. A Pod is the smallest deployable unit; it usually contains a single container for a peer, orderer, or CA, and shares storage and network resources. A Deployment manages a set of identical Pods, ensuring a desired number of replicas and enabling rolling updates to replace Pods with new versions without downtime. A Service provides a stable IP and DNS name for a group of Pods, so clients can connect reliably even when Pods move. Persistent Volumes and Persistent Volume Claims provide durable storage. For Fabric, attach a PVC to a peer Pod so the ledger and state database survive restarts. ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration like core. yaml settings, while Secrets handle sensitive data such as TLS certificates and private keys and are designed for safer consumption by Pods. Each primitive addresses a specific operational need: Pods run processes, Deployments maintain replicas and updates, Services offer stable networking, PV/PVC preserve data durability, and ConfigMaps/Secrets manage configuration and credentials. Misusing a ConfigMap for private keys is a common pitfall; always use Secrets for sensitive material. Keep these mappings in mind as you design Fabric manifests.

A Deployment is the Kubernetes object that manages a ReplicaSet of Pods. It declares the desired replica count and the Pod template, and Kubernetes takes care of creating and replacing Pods to reach that state. This behavior is essential for Fabric peers: a Deployment can ensure multiple peer replicas exist and can perform a rolling update when you change the container image or configuration. To ground this idea, we'll walk through a simple Nginx Deployment manifest you will use in the lab. The manifest sets replicas to two, declares a selector matching labels, and provides a Pod template with container image and port. After applying the manifest with kubectl, you can confirm two Pods are running and then inspect the Deployment status to observe how Kubernetes reconciles the desired state with reality. A common misconception is that a Deployment immediately scales storage or network configuration—Deployments manage Pods; storage is attached through PVCs and network stability is provided by Services. In short, use Deployments to maintain availability, and combine them with PVCs and Services to provide durable storage and stable endpoints for Fabric components.

Networking in Kubernetes is intentional: Pods have ephemeral IPs, so Services provide stable endpoints to reach applications reliably. For Fabric, internal component communication should usually use ClusterIP services, which are only reachable within the cluster and are ideal for peer-to-peer and orderer traffic. When you need external access, such as for client applications or a CA endpoint, NodePort or LoadBalancer service types expose the application outside the cluster. NodePort opens a high-numbered port on every node, while LoadBalancer instructs the cloud provider to provision an external load balancer. A practical example from the hands-on activity uses a Service of type NodePort to access the Nginx Deployment. A common misconception is to expose all Fabric components externally; instead, keep internal Fabric traffic internal and only expose required endpoints. Services also enable DNS names and stable selectors, so even if Pods are rescheduled to different nodes with new IPs, the Service preserves connectivity and simplifies configuration of client applications and other Fabric components. Services and Networking in Fabric means use clusterip for internal fabric communications and nodeport/loadbalancer only when external client access is necessary; services keep connectivity stable despite pod churn.. In practical terms, clusterip, nodeport, and loadbalancer for internal and external access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Persistent Volumes and Persistent Volume Claims are the mechanism Kubernetes provides to decouple storage from ephemeral Pods. A Persistent Volume is a piece of storage in the cluster provisioned by an administrator or dynamically provisioned by storage classes. A Persistent Volume Claim is a request for storage made by a Pod. For Fabric this is critical because ledger files and state databases must survive Pod restarts or Pod rescheduling to other nodes. When a peer Pod mounts a PVC, the cluster ensures the same storage is reattached when the Pod is recreated, preserving ledger continuity. A common misconception is assuming ephemeral container storage is enough; ephemeral storage is lost when a Pod terminates. Design-wise, choose a storage class that matches your durability needs and ensure PVs are sized and backed up appropriately. During testing with Minikube or Kind, you will use local provisioners, but in production managed clusters you will rely on cloud-backed storage classes pointing to durable block or file services. Always verify that the PVC binds successfully before trusting it for ledger persistence. Persistent Volumes and Claims means attach a pvc to peer pods so ledger and state data are stored on a persistent volume that survives pod lifecycle events and node changes.. In practical terms, ensuring ledger data survives pod restarts and rescheduling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ConfigMaps and Secrets let you inject configuration into Pods without baking it into container images. ConfigMaps are intended for non-sensitive key-value pairs like core. yaml or orderer settings; mount them as files or expose them as environment variables. Secrets are similar in structure but are designed for sensitive data: TLS certificates, private keys, and database credentials. Secrets are not encrypted by Kubernetes by default unless you enable additional features, but they are handled differently from ConfigMaps and reduce the chance of accidentally committing secrets into code. For Fabric, place node TLS materials and private keys in Secrets and mount them into the peer or orderer containers. A common pitfall is placing private keys in a ConfigMap or code repository; that creates a security exposure. When designing manifests, reference Secrets in Pod specs and enforce RBAC so only necessary operators can view or mount them. Managing rotation, encryption at rest, and secure delivery of Secrets is part of operational hardening for production Fabric deployments. ConfigMaps and Secrets means use configmaps for non-sensitive configuration and secrets for tls certificates and private keys; treat secrets with stricter operational controls and rotation policies.. In practical terms, managing configuration and sensitive material securely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Minikube runs a single-node cluster inside a VM or container on your workstation, while Kind runs Kubernetes clusters using Docker containers as nodes.
